en: The Scripture on the Dharma-Gate of the Pure Conduct of Upāsikās, Volume One. Recorded by Sengyou as one of the "Extraordinary Scriptures from the Liang Region" attributed to Master Daoan;

appended to the Northern Liang Catalogue. Chapter One: On Cultivating Practice. **Chapter One: On Cultivating Practice** [Text begins]... [The Buddha was dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī... [The Buddha addressed the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs... [At that time, there was an upāsikā named Vimaladattā... [She had previously made offerings to seventy-two thousand Buddhas... [She asked the Buddha, "World-Honored One, how does a woman, having planted roots of goodness under past Buddhas, attain birth in a noble family?"... [The Buddha told Vimaladattā, "If a woman wishes to be born in a noble family, she should cultivate ten kinds of pure conduct... [The Buddha then extensively expounded upon these ten practices... [Vimaladattā, having heard this teaching, attained the stage of non-retrogression... [The Buddha praised her, saying, "Excellent, excellent! You have now truly entered the gate of the Bodhisattva path... [The Buddha further told the bhikṣuṇīs, "You should all learn from Vimaladattā... [At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished preaching this sutra, rose from his seat and departed. [The bhikṣuṇīs, having heard the Buddha’s words, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. [End of Chapter One: On Cultivating Practice.]
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, in the Ghoṣitārāma, the park of Migāramātā, within the Hall of Delight. Thereupon, Viśākhā Mātā, together with fifteen hundred faithful female lay disciples (upāsikās), came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Buddha asked Viśākhā,
"For what reason have you come so early in the morning?
Viśākhā-mātā replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
We have already heard the brief explanation previously given by the Tathāgata regarding the profound, difficult-to-understand, and unsurpassed Dharma called ‘The Pure Conduct of Upāsikās.

We only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and extensively expound and analyze the subtle characteristics of this Dharma, so that having heard this teaching, we may enjoy peace, security, and happiness throughout the long night of saṃsāra—in the heavens and among humans, and even until the attainment of Bodhi.”
The Buddha said to Visākhā:
“Excellent, excellent,
noble woman!”
"In immeasurable kalpas of the past, you always delighted in hearing the Dharma; together with your retinue, you once sought from me an extensive exposition.
When Viśākhā heard these words concerning her past causes and conditions, she was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will expound this for me, so that I may attain understanding.
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!”
I shall now explain this briefly for you.
Good woman!
In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī, and its king was named Brahmadatta; the king’s queen was named Bhadrā.
The king had a daughter named Padmā, who was of upright appearance and possessed a gentle and virtuous nature;
she was intelligent and discerning, delighted in extensive learning,
and was diligent and courageous, constantly cultivating wholesome deeds.
He was highly proficient in worldly arts and crafts and was always cherished and respected by his parents.

At that time, there was a brahmin on Mount Himavat named Narada who diligently practiced the holy life and attained the five supernormal powers; he constantly expounded the various dharmas to the great assembly, and his fame spread far and wide throughout the four quarters.

At that time, having heard from her virtuous friend such praise of the brahmin’s supernatural powers—his merit being immeasurable and his constant proclamation of the sublime Dharma to the great assembly—the woman felt joy arise in her heart and thought to herself:

"Virtuous persons are difficult to encounter, the Dharma is difficult to hear, and this physical life is difficult to preserve; therefore, I should now go quickly to pay him homage and inquire about the Dharma."
Having had this thought, he went to his parents and addressed them, saying:

"I have heard people praise the brahmin for his cultivation of the Way and virtue, which are most sublime. I only pray that my parents will grant me permission to go to that brahmin to hear and receive the flavor of the Dharma!"

The parents replied, "You are but a child, raised within the deep palace; by nature you are delicate and have never before gone outside. The Snowy Mountains are remote and distant, and the road is perilous and difficult; how could you possibly reach them now?"

"In my country there are many venerable brahmins whose spiritual wisdom is peerless and who are well able to proclaim the profound and sublime Dharma. I shall request them to enter the palace for you to discourse on the Way; you may ask whatever you wish, so there is no need for you to leave!"
The woman requested again, saying:
"The elder brahmins of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī all revere and esteem his spiritual arts; I only pray that you will grant me permission to hear the essentials of the Dharma!"
Out of affection, the king did not go against his wish and granted it with some reluctance.

At that time, the father-king immediately commanded his four ministers and the court ladies of the palace to prepare all the ornaments and offerings until they were complete. The ministers addressed the king, saying:
"Whatever Your Majesty has commanded has now been fully prepared."
Thereupon, the princess thought to herself, "I seek to hear the Dharma;
now is precisely the right time!
She then took fifteen hundred court ladies and attendants from the palace, carrying incense and flowers, and went to the brahmin to listen to the Dharma.
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"The princess at that time was you yourself;
the brahmin of the Snowy Mountains was I myself."
“In the past you requested an extensive teaching, and now it is the same.
I shall, for your sake, analyze and expound the Dharma-gate of Pure Conduct!
Viśākhā, mother of Mṛgāra, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
Out of great compassion and pity for sentient beings, we pray that you will explain this for us; we shall practice it accordingly.
The Buddha said to Viśākhā:
“Listen attentively!
I shall now extensively expound and analyze for you the Dharma-gate of the Pure Conduct of Upāsikās.
Such a teaching is protected and remembered by all Buddhas; you should now diligently cultivate and study it.”
"Viśākhā! If a virtuous woman abandons evil associates, draws near to spiritual friends, and makes offerings to those worthy of offerings, this is called the pure conduct of an upāsikā."
“To be born in a favorable land through the influence of past causes, and to dwell there with a well-settled body, is also called pure conduct.
To make offerings to one’s parents, to serve one’s husband, and to care for one’s children is also called pure conduct.”
"Do not conceive a sense of lightness regarding even minor offenses; performing what ought to be done in its proper sequence is also called pure conduct.
Constantly delighting in giving, practicing the rites of the Dharma, and cherishing one's friends and kin is also called pure conduct."
"To abstain from drinking alcohol, to refrain from all evil deeds, and to constantly cultivate kind speech is also called pure conduct.
To possess extensive learning and skills, to be well-trained in dignified deportment, and to investigate what one has heard so as not to let it be forgotten is also called pure conduct."
"To be reverent and respectful, to have few desires and be content, and to be able to repay kindness received—this is also called pure conduct.
To be unmoved by the eight worldly dharmas and to maintain a joyful countenance—this is also called pure conduct."

"If the mind is free from sorrow and distress, and one constantly attains peace and stability; if one can thus remain without retreat in all matters and bring all activities to rest, this is also called pure conduct.
To be able to give rise to no indolence regarding wholesome dharmas and swiftly realize unsurpassed liberation and nirvana—this too is called pure conduct."
"To practice patience according to one's words, to delight in seeing śramaṇas, to act with rectitude in body, and to rely upon the great shade—this is also called pure conduct.
To be able to burn away afflictions with the fire of wisdom, to be fully endowed with wholesome dharmas, and to be courageous and never retreat—this is also called pure conduct."
"Not slandering others, not inflicting corporal punishment, well-guarding the sense faculties, and restraining the mind so it is not distracted—this is also called pure conduct.
Having a straightforward mind free from greed, always delighting in secluded places, and practicing with diligent effort without ever regressing—this is also called pure conduct."
"To advance upon the path to enlightenment without retreating, to loathe the three realms as one would a corpse, and to contemplate them deeply—this is also called pure conduct.

To constantly delight in relinquishing the body that is so difficult to give up, to be well able to maintain the precepts that are so difficult to uphold, and to delight in cultivating meditative concentration without distraction—this is also called pure conduct."

"Infinite sentient beings conceive thoughts of retreat regarding the path to enlightenment, yet I am able to advance all who advance; I do not retreat, remaining thus whether walking or staying—this is called pure conduct."

"All sentient beings burn away and destroy their roots of goodness, yet I cause them to grow; that which people delight in producing, I now extinguish; though birth and death are limitless, I have reached their end—this is also called pure conduct."
Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, Visākhā, her mother, was filled with joy and exultation, having attained what she had never experienced before. She addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, how many practices are there further in the dharma-gate for upāsikās?”
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"There are ten practices that you should cultivate and study.
What are these ten?"
First, seeing the fault of stinginess and greed, they delight in practicing generosity;
second, seeing the faults of the five faculties, they delight in upholding the prohibitive precepts;
third, seeing the faults of the household life, they delight in seeking to leave home.
Fourth, seeing the fault of doubt and confusion, they delight in cultivating wisdom;
fifth, seeing the fault of indolence, they delight in diligent perseverance;
sixth, seeing the fault of anger and resentment, they delight in practicing patience.
Seventh, seeing the fault of false speech, one delights in loyalty and trustworthiness;
eighth, seeing the fault of a distracted mind, one constantly delights in meditative concentration;
ninth, seeing the fault of the suffering of transgressions, one delights in loving-kindness and compassion.
"Tenth, seeing the faults of suffering and pleasure, one should delight in practicing the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"From giving, one attains great wealth; One is able to relinquish even the beloved body."
Leaving desire behind, one goes forth into homelessness; Upholding the precepts, one restrains the sense faculties.
Cultivating training, one attains wisdom; With diligence, one cuts off indolence;
With patience, one eliminates anger; Speaking truthfully, one is free from falsehood.
If one encounters the eight worldly dharmas, one remains steadfast with an unmoving mind.
Always delighting in meditative concentration, one is forever free from distraction.
With compassion, one benefits sentient beings; cultivating equanimity, one abandons both suffering and pleasure.
"If one can practice this Dharma, they are called truly courageous;
having reached the shore of the ocean of Dharma, they shall realize the path to Bodhi.
Upon hearing what the Buddha had spoken, Mother Viśākhā felt great joy in her heart and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How many things should one initially distance oneself from?
Furthermore, how many dharmas should one draw near to?”
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"There are fifty-eight dharmas that one should cultivate and study, and which one should also distance oneself from. What are they?"
That is to say:
one should distance oneself from all impure dharmas and draw near to pure dharmas;
one should abandon unwholesome dharmas and draw near to wholesome dharmas.
One should not raise or nurture them;
one should not go to places where they dwell, nor approach them with intimacy;
as for those places where one ought to go, one should indeed go there.
That which should not be done, one must never do falsely;
that which should be done, one should perform with skillful means;
and what is obtained through unrighteous means, one should not employ.
One should enjoy what is obtained in accordance with the Dharma;
well-disciplining body and mind, one should always delight in solitary places;
abandoning deceit and hypocrisy, one should practice right speech.
One should cultivate weariness toward laziness and delight in the practice of diligence;
skillfully restrain the sense faculties so as not to allow them to become heedless;
and first show humility and respect with one's mind, abandoning all arrogance.
Constantly practicing patience, they do not give rise to anger;
they do not engage in disputes themselves, but skillfully bring harmony to the assembly;
they abandon concealment and do not dwell in a state of hiding their faults.
He abandons frivolous speech and dwells in meaningful speech;
he abandons wrong livelihood and sustains himself through right livelihood;
he is skillfully mindful of his body when receiving food and drink.
One does not delight in seeking much, but dwells in fewness of desires;
one abandons harshness and dwells on the ground of gentleness;
one cultivates soft speech and remains far removed from coarse words.
Abandoning unhappiness, one dwells in a state of happiness;
abandoning those of differing views, one dwells together with those of similar class;
abandoning places where there is no inquiry, one goes to places where one may consult and inquire.
One becomes weary of and detached from the three realms, dwelling in non-attachment to the three realms;
one relinquishes all conditioned activities, dwelling in non-action;
and one abandons the view of self, practicing and studying the dharma of emptiness.
"Viśākhā! These fifty-eight primary dharmas are thus; you should practice them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“If all that is to be learned, from beginning to end, without exception,
is practiced by remaining far from what should be avoided and drawing near to what should be cultivated, one will attain peace and happiness.
Having completed the training in all dharmas, all one’s aspirations will be fulfilled.”
Because they relinquish their bodies and lives, they realize the unsurpassed path.
If one trains in this manner, regarding the dharma-gate of pure conduct,
such a person is neither a śrāvaka nor a pratyekabuddha, yet is not a bodhisattva who has already attained realization.
"Throughout immeasurable eons, one shall praise his merits.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, the mother Viśākhā was filled with great joy and asked further:
"World-Honored One!..."
“How many kinds of dharma-gates for pure conduct are there that are called ‘great practices’?
The Buddha said,
“There are three great practices that you should cultivate.”
What are called the three great practices?
First, great faith; second, great diligence;
[and third, great wisdom].
"Third is great wisdom.
"World-Honored One,
what is great faith?"
The Buddha said:
"Great faith is faith in the Buddha.
That the Buddha is the Bhagavān, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān—this is called great faith."
What is great diligence?

If one can cultivate the practice of diligence therein, abandoning and distancing oneself from all unwholesome dharmas, and correctly embracing all wholesome dharmas, exerting oneself with vigor and without ceasing within those wholesome dharmas—this is called great diligence.
What is great wisdom?
If a person, with the eye of wisdom, perceives the phenomena of arising and ceasing—that which the noble ones have transcended as impermanence, suffering, and exhaustion—this is called great wisdom.
"This is what is called the three kinds of great practices.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"With great faith in common, Deeply attached and never departing, All practices are fully perfected."
They seek awakening;
with great diligence, firm and difficult to relinquish, having fulfilled their arduous cultivation, they seek awakening.
Together with great wisdom, they attain ultimate clarity; possessing the pāramitās, they seek bodhi.
Once the initial dharma has increased, they come to know their great renown;
when that increase reaches its consummation, they act in accordance with their practice. Because of this knowledge, they understand the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma).
When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, Mother Viśākhā felt great joy in her heart and asked further with increased devotion:
"World-Honored One!
Regarding the Dharma-gate of the pure conduct of upāsikās, how many more practices are there for progressing toward the stage of Buddhahood?"
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"There are further four practices by which one attains the stage of a Buddha.
What are these four?"
First, ardent and diligent vigor;
second, unconfused wisdom;
third, entering meditative concentration without regression.
Fourth, practicing loving-kindness to benefit sentient beings.
Viśākhā! By means of these four dharmas, one advances toward the stage of Buddhahood.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Exerting oneself with joy in diligence, Possessing wisdom free from delusion,
Advancing steadily without turning back, Practicing loving-kindness to benefit all beings.”
"By means of these four dharmas, one realizes sarvajñā (all-knowledge).
When the Buddha had finished speaking this verse, the mother Viśākhā felt great joy in her heart and asked further:
"World-Honored One!"
Furthermore, in how many dharmas does one abide to attain contemplation?
How do these dharmas assemble without dispersal?
And how many matters are there in the initial application of these dharmas?
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
“One attains contemplation by abiding in four dharmas, namely: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

Within these, the gathering of dharmas is without dispersal; that is to say, one attains the wisdom of the śrāvaka, the wisdom of the pratyekabuddha, the wisdom of sarvajña, and the wisdom of the Buddha.”

Regarding the initial application of the methods, there are thirty-two contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-dharma*), namely: mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, mindfulness of the Saṃgha,
mindfulness of the precepts, mindfulness of generosity, mindfulness of the devas, mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (inhalation and exhalation), and the contemplation of the perception of cessation,
the contemplation of the perception of the body, the contemplation of the perception of tranquility, and the contemplation of earth, water, fire, and...
The perception of wind; the perception of observing blue, yellow, red, and white; the perception of observing empty space; the perception of observing the sphere of consciousness;
the perception of observing a bloated corpse; the perception of observing a putrid corpse; the perception of observing a perforated and leaking corpse; the perception of observing a festering corpse;
the perception of observing a dismembered corpse scattered in various places; the perception of observing bones strewn hither and thither; and the perception of observing moist bones.
The contemplation of the skeleton, the contemplation of the color of the skeleton, the contemplation of the impermanence of all things,
and the contemplation of the selflessness of all phenomena— these are called the thirty-two methods of contemplation.
The four immeasurable minds are called abiding in the attainment of contemplation;
the wisdom of the śrāvakas, the wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas, the wisdom of sarvajña, and the wisdom of the Buddha—these are called the gathering of dharmas without dispersal.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"If one observes below, one attains the wisdom of a śrāvaka; if one skillfully cultivates middle observation, one attains the wisdom of a pratyekabuddha;
if upper observation is perfected, one attains the wisdom of bodhi."
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, Mother Viśākhā was filled with great joy and asked further:
"World-Honored One,
regarding the dharma-gate of impurity, how does one dwell the mind so as to swiftly leave behind afflictions and penetrate the six gates?"
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"There are thirty-two dharma-gates through which the mind may dwell with delight amidst impurity; by swiftly departing from afflictions, one then penetrates the six gates."
What are the thirty-two dharma-gates? They are:

within the body there are hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, tendons, bones, fat, grease, marrow, brain, heart, kidneys, liver, gallbladder, large intestine, small intestine, spleen, lungs, stomach, intestines, pus, blood, phlegm, sweat, nasal mucus, saliva, spittle, tears, feces, and urine—all these impurities.
"Viśākhā!

These are the thirty-two contemplations on impurity, which cause the mind to delight in dwelling within the dharma-gate of pure conduct, swiftly abandon the afflictions, and attain mastery over the six sense-gates."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Just as the currents of rivers Flow together into the great ocean, So too is the flow of contemplation within the Dharma-gate."
“Skillfully observing the coarse and the subtle, the pure and the impure, through the dharma of unsurpassed wisdom, the Buddha has fully realized all things.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these verses, Mother Viśākhā was filled with great joy and asked further:
“World-Honored One!”
"How many attachments do bodhisattvas have toward the dharma-gate of pure conduct that cause them to dwell in the world and fail to attain liberation?
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"Regarding the dharma-gate of pure conduct, there were seven fetters by which former bodhisattvas dwelt in the world."
What are the seven?
First, if I have attained liberation while the world has not yet been liberated, I desire to liberate it;
second, if I have attained deliverance while the world has not yet been delivered, I desire to deliver it.
Third, if I have already awakened while the world has not yet awakened, I desire to awaken it;
fourth, if I have already been disciplined while the world has not yet been disciplined, I desire to discipline it;
fifth, if I have already attained peace while the world has not yet attained peace, I desire to bring it peace.
Sixth, if I attain the Way while the world has not yet attained it, I desire to guide them;
seventh, if I have already attained nirvana while the world has not yet attained it, I desire to cause them to enter into nirvana.
"Viśākhā! These are the seven kinds of attachment of a bodhisattva; dwelling in the world, they do not attain liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Having crossed over, you lead sentient beings across; having been liberated, you liberate sentient beings;
having awakened, you awaken sentient beings; having been tamed, you tame sentient beings;
having attained peace, you bring peace to sentient beings; having reached guidance, you guide sentient beings."
I have already attained nirvāṇa, and cause all sentient beings to attain nirvāṇa.
The triple world is like a house on fire; craving is like a net of mud.
Having extinguished and severed them all, I have realized the path of Bodhi.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the Mother Viśākhā was filled with great joy and asked further:
"World-Honored One!
How many wholesome practices must be cultivated through this Dharma-gate of Pure Conduct for all dharmas to be fulfilled?"
The Buddha said:
"Cultivate the three types of wholesome conduct to bring all dharmas to fulfillment.
What are these three types of wholesome conduct?"
First, wholesome conduct of body;
second, wholesome conduct of speech;
third, wholesome conduct of mind.
When these three types of wholesome conduct are fulfilled, they cause all dharmas to be fulfilled; that is to say, one attains the fulfillment of generosity,
the fulfillment of ethical discipline, the fulfillment of renunciation, the fulfillment of wisdom, the fulfillment of diligence, the fulfillment of patience,
the fulfillment of truthfulness, the fulfillment of vows, and the fulfillment of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.

...attaining the fulfillment of the four contemplations, attaining the fulfillment of the four meditative concentrations, attaining the fulfillment of the four bases of psychic power, attaining the fulfillment of the five faculties, attaining the fulfillment of the five powers,
attaining the fulfillment of the seven factors of enlightenment, attaining the fulfillment of the eightfold noble path, attaining the fulfillment of the nine knowledges,
attaining the fulfillment of the knowledge of the ten powers, and attaining the fulfillment of the knowledge of the path of the stream-enterer. Attaining the stream-...
He fulfills the knowledge of the fruit of stream-entry; he fulfills the knowledge of the path to once-returning; he fulfills the knowledge of the fruit of once-returning;
he fulfills the knowledge of the path to non-returning; he fulfills the knowledge of the fruit of non-returning; he fulfills the knowledge of the path to arhatship;
he fulfills the knowledge of the fruit of arhatship; thus he fulfills the four knowledges.

That is to say: the fulfillment of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), the knowledge of what is yet to be known (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of names and words, and the knowledge of others' minds; the fulfillment of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), the fulfillment of the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), the fulfillment of the twin miraculous powers (yamaka-prātihārya), the fulfillment of the knowledge of the samādhi of great compassion (mahāmaitrī-samādhi-jñāna), the fulfillment of all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), and the fulfillment of unimpeded knowledge (asaṅga-jñāna).
"Viśākhā! This is called the fulfillment of the three types of wholesome conduct, which brings all dharmas to fulfillment.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Having cultivated the three types of wholesome conduct, all dharmas are fulfilled;
having fulfilled all dharmas, one realizes the path to Bodhi.
When the Buddha had spoken this verse, the Mother Viśākhā was filled with great joy and asked further:
“World-Honored One!
How many types of great beings’ mindfulness are there in the Dharma-gate of Pure Conduct?
The Buddha said:
“There are eight recollections of great persons. What are the eight?
First, having few desires, rather than not having few desires;”
Second, contentment, not discontent;
third, tranquility, not lack of tranquility;
fourth, seclusion, not lack of seclusion.
Fifth, diligence that is not non-diligence;
sixth, meditative concentration that is not non-concentration;
seventh, wisdom that is not non-wisdom.
Eighth, they are unimpeded, yet not non-unimpeded.
Viśākhā, these are called the eight recollections of a great person.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Stabilize all thoughts through skillful concentration; be mindful of what is not wholesome.
If you disparage such thoughts, you will give rise to weary detachment."
"Stabilizing all mindfulness well, Mindfulness of what is not wholesome dharma, Contemplating and refining the characteristics of dharmas, One attains progress toward the Unsurpassed.

Chapter Two: On Cultivation and Study The Scripture on the Dharma Gate of Pure Conduct for Upāsikās, Chapter Two: On Cultivation and Study. After the Buddha had spoken these verses, the Mother of Viśākhā was filled with great joy and asked further with increased reverence:
"World-Honored One!"
"How should a beginner bodhisattva practice and train in the dharma-gate of pure conduct to attain bodhi?
The Buddha said,
"A beginner bodhisattva has fifty modes of training through which they attain bodhi."
What are the fifty? They are:
deeply entering the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), neither abandoning nor diminishing it, not falling away and not regressing;
training in the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), training in extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), training in dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*), and training in subduing all Māras.
They study the light; they practice and study the marks and signs of a Buddha; they practice and study the prohibitions and precepts; they practice and study samādhi; they practice and study prajñā;
they practice and study mahāprajñā; they practice and study wholesome conduct; they practice and study great wholesome conduct;
they practice and study physical forms; they practice and study non-dual speech; they practice and study the bases of psychic power; they practice and study...
Training in the higher bases of psychic power; training in the great bases of psychic power; training in the sublime bases of psychic power;
training in the mental formations; training in the completed mental formations; training in the great mental formations; training in that which is ruled by the Buddha; training in mastery;
training in the characteristics of the Buddha-mind; and training in the characteristics of the perfected mind.
...to train in the supernormal powers, to train in the great supernormal powers, to train in reality,
to train in the governance of the True Dharma so that it may endure for a long time, to train in the ultimate state, to train in the Buddha-fields,
to train in the lifespan of the Buddhas, to train in the Bodhi tree, to train in the lotus, and to train in the Buddhas.
To study the teaching of the Dharma; to study the Great Wheel of Dharma; to study the turning of the Wheel of Dharma;
to study spiritual friends; to study not abandoning sentient beings; to study the perfection of the hands; to study the garments of the *kalpavṛkṣa* tree;
to study the lion throne; to study the bed for lying on the right side; and to study the flavors of food consumed by the Buddha.
...to train in the *viśeṣa*, and to train in the water-like characteristic of the Tathāgata. Viśākha!
These are the fifty dharmas of training that a bodhisattva at the initial stage should train in deeply, not abandoning, not diminishing, not falling away, and not regressing; you should know this!
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Endowed with all practices, he seeks the dharma of tranquility;
his radiance illuminates the Buddha-fields, for the sake of compassion for sentient beings.”
"Guiding all sentient beings, To cross over the perils of the three realms;
All dharmas are inexhaustible, And the Tathāgata has already reached that state.
When the World-Honored One had spoken this verse, Mother Viśākhā was filled with great joy and asked further:
“World-Honored One!
How many rays of light does the Tathāgata possess, and how should a novice bodhisattva practice?
The Buddha told Viśākha:
“The Tathāgata possesses six kinds of radiance.
What are these six?
First is blue light;”
Second, yellow light;
third, red light;
fourth, white light.
Fifth, crimson light;
sixth, radiant illumination. Vaiśākha!
These are called the six kinds of light of the Tathāgata.
How should a beginner bodhisattva practice to attain this light? Viśākha!

In order to attain blue radiance, a bodhisattva constantly makes offerings with blue flowers, blue ointments, powdered incense, blue cotton cloth, and blue jewels; when entering meditative concentration, they always contemplate the color blue, and having performed these acts, they make the vow that in a future life they may attain blue radiance.
How does a bodhisattva practice and train in the yellow light?

They constantly make offerings with yellow flowers, yellow ointments, powdered incense, yellow cotton cloth, and yellow jewels; when entering meditative concentration, they always contemplate the color yellow, and having performed these acts, they make a vow that in future lives they may attain the yellow light.
How does a bodhisattva practice and study the red light?

They constantly make offerings with red flowers, red ointments, powdered incense, red cotton cloth, and red jewels; when entering meditative concentration, they always contemplate the color red, and having performed these acts, they make the vow that in a future life they shall obtain the red light.
How does a bodhisattva practice and train in white light?

Constantly making offerings with white flowers, white ointments, powdered incense, white cotton cloth, and white jewels; when entering meditative concentration, always contemplating the color white; and having performed these acts, making the vow that in future lives one may attain white light.
How does a bodhisattva practice and train in the red light?

They constantly make offerings with red flowers, red ointments, powdered incense, red cotton cloth, and red jewels; when entering meditative concentration, they always contemplate the color red; having performed these acts, they make the vow that in future lives they shall obtain the red light.
How does a bodhisattva practice the cultivation of radiant illumination?

They constantly make offerings with flowers of light, ointments and powdered incenses of light, cotton cloths of light, and jewels of light; when entering meditative concentration, they constantly contemplate light, and having performed these acts, they make the vow that in future lives they may attain radiant illumination.
"Viśākhā! This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation and study of the six kinds of light of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The Buddha's light has six kinds: blue, yellow, red, white, and crimson;
its radiant marks shine most brilliantly.
If there are people of wisdom, they should always practice with diligence."
If you delight in wondrous forms and light, you should train in the vast practice;
with flowers, incense, and lamps as offerings, constantly bestow them upon the Unsurpassed Honored One.
By training in these six kinds of practices, all your aspirations will be fulfilled.
After the Buddha had spoken these verses, Mother Viśākhā was filled with great joy and asked further:
"World-Honored One!
How many kinds of marks of a Great Man are there? How should a novice Bodhisattva practice and train?"
The Buddha said:

"There are thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and there are twenty practices cultivated by a Bodhisattva; when these accord with the marks of a Great Man, one attains the two paths, and there is nothing further."
What are the two paths?
If one is a householder, one may become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), ruling over the four quarters of the world, subduing all nations, followed by the seven treasures:

first, the golden wheel treasure; second, the white elephant treasure; third, the white horse treasure; fourth, the mani-jewel treasure; fifth, the jade woman treasure; sixth, the steward treasure; and seventh, the military commander treasure. Furthermore, he has a thousand sons who are brave, robust, and majestic, capable of subduing enemies and foes throughout the reaches of the great ocean, bringing them under submission through the Dharma without the use of weapons.
If one leaves the household life, they shall attain Buddhahood, becoming the most honored and supreme among gods and humans, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
What are these thirty-two marks?
That is to say: his body is golden in color; his halo extends one fathom and resembles molten gold; his Brahma-body is square and upright; behind his neck is the radiance of the sun;
he has a fleshly protuberance on the crown of his head; his hair is deep blue-black; and the Buddha’s body is perfectly full like a *nyagrodha* tree.
The *kūlaka* tree; the tuft of hair between the eyebrows is like *tūla* cotton; both eyes blink simultaneously; the eyelashes are deep blue; the tongue can cover the face;
the Brahma-voice has eight qualities like the song of the *kalaviṅka*;
the mouth has forty teeth, which are white, even, and closely set; the jaw is like that of a lion; and the skin is so fine and thin that it does not retain dust.
He is free from impurities; from each and every pore grows a single hair, deep blue in color, fine and soft, all curling to the right;
he has the chest of a lion; on his breast is the *svastika* mark; the seven parts of his body are full; his hands and feet are joined by webbing; his fingers are slender and long;
when his hands are closed, they reach his elbows; when standing upright, his hands extend past his knees; his male organ is retracted like that of a horse; and his legs are straight and well-knit.
Antelope calves, the mark of the casket base, the thousand-spoked wheel, and long heels—
these are called the thirty-two marks of a Great Man’s body.
"Viśākhā!..."
What are the twenty matters for cultivating the marks of a Great Man?

When the Tathāgata was formerly a common person, he achieved steadfastness in wholesome dharmas and maintained them without wavering; he performed wholesome deeds of body, wholesome deeds of speech, and wholesome thoughts of mind. He shared all his giving with sentient beings, strictly observed the prohibitive precepts, constantly abided in the *poṣadha*, and made offerings to his parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders of long-standing virtue, and his six kinds of relatives.

Having practiced all wholesome dharmas to their full extent, having cultivated them to fulfillment and accumulated them to great heights, from throughout immeasurable births and deaths until reaching the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), he constantly enjoys celestial pleasures with sovereign mastery over lifespan, physical strength, royal authority, renown, form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch.

Having enjoyed these celestial pleasures, he descends to be born among humans and attains the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*): his soles are flat, and when he walks, his feet adhere firmly to the ground; when he lifts his feet, they rise up together, and the insteps of his feet are prominent like the shell of a tortoise.
By virtue of these marks, if one remains a householder, one becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King;

if one leaves the household life, one attains Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, forever severing birth and death, and attaining the eternal bliss of Nirvana, which cannot be destroyed by internal or external enemies—whether Brahmā, Māra, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas—and such a person is called a Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Being pliant and supple toward all dharmas, Constantly maintaining the fasts and prohibitions,
With a mind of equanimity in giving, One deeply contemplates the dharma of impermanence."
All the deeds one has performed, one upholds with a firm mind;
by virtue of these deeds, one is constantly reborn among gods and humans.
Having experienced the pleasures of the heavens, one returns once more to be born among humans.
Receiving worldly blessings and rewards, he attains level soles;
wherever he treads upon the earth, it all makes contact with his feet, rising up to meet him as he walks.
Whether living at home or having left the home life, all possess such marks as these.
Whether Brahmā or Māra, śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas,
all enemies whatsoever have been utterly subdued.
Having left the household life to practice the Way, he has cut off the source of birth and death.
"All practices having been fulfilled, he has attained the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Furthermore, Viśākhā, how does one cultivate the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel?"
In the past, when the Tathāgata was an ordinary person, he bore the burden of sentient beings, removing their terrors and bestowing upon them the joy of fearlessness.
Whatever he gave in alms, he shared entirely with all beings; the accumulated merit he amassed was so lofty and vast that it could not be measured or calculated.
Having passed away from this life, he will be reborn in the heavens where he constantly experiences sublime bliss; thus it continues in succession, immeasurable and boundless.
When descending to be born in the world, he will obtain the marks of a Great Man, including the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of his feet, which are fully perfected like wheels of pure gold.

Having attained these marks, if he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, followed by the seven treasures, and constantly surrounded by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, householders, ministers, elders, and the fourfold army;

if he leaves the home life, he will attain Buddhahood, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, who will all revere and honor him with respect.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, Transmigrating through the three realms,
I have borne the burdens of sentient beings' happiness, In order to eliminate their places of fear."
Guarding well without ceasing, through these meritorious deeds,
one shall always be reborn among humans and devas until reaching the stage of "one birth remaining" (ekajātipratibaddha).
With the thousand-spoked wheels on the soles of his two feet, their radiance shines like a golden wheel.
Through the retribution of a thousand deeds, he is prophesied to become the Honored One among men;
surrounded by a great assembly, he shall subdue all demonic adversaries.
Had he been born into the Kṣatriya caste, he would have become a Wheel-Turning King.
If one leaves the household life to study the Way and attains the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One,
then devas, humans, asuras, mahoragas, and others—
quadrupeds and non-humans alike— all shall revere and make offerings to them.
"His fame fills the ten directions; he is a field of merit for all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā, how does one cultivate the three marks of a Great Man?"

When the Tathāgata was formerly an ordinary person, he did not harm sentient beings; he abandoned the thought of killing, did not employ sticks or whips, and did not keep any weapons whatsoever. He constantly gave rise to a sense of shame and remorse, and cultivated loving-kindness and compassion.
The accumulated karma is lofty and remote, inconceivable, spanning immeasurable births and deaths until reaching the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood;
descending to be born among humans, he attains three marks of a great man:
first, his heels are long.
Second, the fingers are slender and long;
third, the Brahma-body is rounded and straight.
Because of these marks, it is predicted that his lifespan will be long; he manifests the sign of enduring residence and is likewise protected in his life, never meeting an untimely death.

If one leaves the household life, they shall attain Buddhahood with a long lifespan; no one among the devas, humans, śramaṇas, or brahmins in all the worlds will be able to harm the Tathāgata’s life span.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"All fear death and dread the sword and staff; Taking oneself as the analogy, do not wield the staff.
Therefore, remain far removed from such thoughts; By this virtuous conduct, one is born in the heavens."
Having experienced immeasurable bliss as the karmic fruit of heaven, when his lifespan ends, he is reborn below and attains three marks:
his fingers and heels are long, and his Brahma-body is full; when placed upon the ground, they rest like a golden tortoise;
his feet are soft, slender, and long like golden pestles; and his body is radiant like Mount Sumeru.
The three marks certify his attainment as the Honored One among gods and men, and they also signify the long lifespan of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Viśākhā, how does one cultivate the seven marks of fullness?

In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, when the Tathāgata was a common person, he constantly acted as a donor, diligently practicing generosity by providing delicacies, food and drink, various sweet fruits, and fragrant, delicious beverages.
Having accumulated merit so vast and immeasurable that it cannot be calculated, he will enjoy celestial pleasures until reaching the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood;
when descending to be born in the human world, he will attain the mark of the seven parts being full:
his shoulders, neck, arms, and feet will all be perfectly rounded.
By virtue of these marks, if he remains a householder, he will become a wheel-turning sage-king (cakravartin) and obtain the most excellent flavors in the world;
if he leaves the household life, he will become a Buddha, and the food and drink he receives will be the most supreme among all flavors in the heavens and the human realm.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Eating, chewing, licking, and tasting the unsurpassed flavors— The donor constantly practices such deeds;
By virtue of these immeasurable wholesome actions, They enjoy happiness within the Nanda Garden."
Through the retribution of karma, he was born into this world; He attained the seven places of excellence among the marks of a Great Man.
His hands and feet were soft and supple beyond compare; By virtue of these marks, he obtained the supreme flavors.
Whether at home or having left the home life, it was always thus; The Tathāgata has forever severed the outflows of the triple world.
Therefore, he attains the status of the Unsurpassed Honored One. Furthermore, Viśākhā,
how does one cultivate the mark of hands and feet that are soft and supple, with webbed fingers and toes?
When the Buddha was formerly an ordinary person, he constantly gathered in sentient beings through the four means of integration—
generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation— and never refused anyone who came to him with a request.
Having accumulated karma so vast and lofty as to reach the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (ekajātipratibaddha), he constantly experiences celestial bliss;
when descending to be born in the world, he attains two marks of a Great Man:
first, his hands and feet are soft and supple; second, his fingers and toes are joined by a web-like membrane.
By virtue of these marks, if he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King who governs the four continents;

if he leaves the household life, he will attain the status of a Dharma King who skillfully gathers and sustains all immeasurable sentient beings—monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans alike.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Cultivating generosity and kind speech, Practicing beneficial conduct and cooperation,
Constantly employing the four means of integration, One gathers the assembly without exception."
By virtue of these karmic deeds, one is constantly reborn among gods and humans;
when descending to be born in the world, one attains two marks of a Great Man:
the hands and feet are entirely soft and supple, and both are endowed with webbed fingers and toes.
Exquisite, extremely fine and thin, with a yellow exterior and a red interior;
because of these two characteristics, the householder wheel-turning king,
if he transforms others through the Dharma of goodness, will cause all to follow his conduct.
Firmly upholding the precepts without transgression, he joyfully praises the Holy King;
his bestowal of grace is peerless, and his compassionate moisture pervades the four quarters.
If one abandons the five desires and leaves the household life, one shall attain Buddhahood.
He preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, and all who hear it receive it upon the crown of their heads.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā,
how does he practice so as to attain the Tathāgata’s mark of feet that are straight and level, and body hairs that curl upward?"
The Buddha told Viśākhā:

"In the past, when I was still an ordinary person, I constantly benefited sentient beings with wholesome dharmas and always practiced the gift of Dharma; from the beginning, I never spoke words that were meaningless."
By virtue of this karma, his merit increases and expands until he reaches the stage of being "born only once more" (ekajātipratibaddha);
when descending to be born in the world, he attains two marks of a great man:
first, his legs are straight and shapely, with the ankle bones not protruding.
Second, his body hairs curl upward at their tips.

Because of this mark, if he remains in the household life, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), the most honored, exalted, sublime, and superior among men, who finds joy and happiness amidst the five desires, followed and guarded by the seven treasures and a thousand sons;

if he renounces his household affairs to enter the mountains and study the Way, he will attain Buddhahood, becoming the most honored and supreme among devas and humans, without equal, and revered and respected by all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Always by means of wholesome dharmas, benefit sentient beings; Always by means of wholesome speech, instruct and guide sentient beings;
Always by means of wholesome power, attend and serve sentient beings."
Rejoicing in joy and happiness, they constantly practice the gift of Dharma and are free from envy.
By virtue of this karma, having accumulated immeasurable conduct, they descend to be born among humans and attain the marks of a Great Man.
The calves are straight and firm, with no protruding ankle bones;
the hair on the head grows in tufts, all curling to the right.
If he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning King, ruling over the four continents.
"If one leaves the household life, they shall attain Buddhahood, becoming the most honored and supreme among devas and humans.
Furthermore, Viśākhā!"
How does one cultivate the mark of the deer-like calves?

In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, when the Tathāgata was still an ordinary person, he diligently and skillfully taught others all treatises, dignified deportment, arts and crafts, medical prescriptions, and incantations. He taught them to maintain the prohibitive precepts in their entirety and constantly reflected:
"How may I cause people to well understand the meaning and intent, so that they quickly attain thorough penetration without giving rise to weariness or feelings of aversion?"
"By virtue of this karma, he diligently accumulated merit until reaching the stage of 'one birth remaining' (ekajātipratibaddha), constantly enjoying celestial pleasures;
when descending to be born in the world, he attained the marks of a Great Man, including the mark of having calves like those of a deer."

If they remain as householders, they shall become Wheel-Turning Sage Kings, ruling over the four continents, and all requisites for their needs and offerings will be swiftly obtained according to their thoughts;
if they renounce the household life, they shall attain Buddhahood, and all requisites for their needs and offerings among devas and humans will likewise be swiftly obtained.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Teach all the scriptures, The arts and crafts, as well as incantations and spells;
In medical prescriptions, examine all ailments, And constantly maintain this reflection:"
How can one quickly achieve success, remain untiring in training,
and in turn teach others?
Accumulating immeasurable merit until reaching the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood.
He has attained the marks and signs of a Great Man; his calves are like those of a deer, slender, beautiful, and perfectly rounded;
his skin is fine, thin, and soft, and the hairs upon it all grow turning to the right.
He is recorded as becoming the Honored One among men; as a wheel-turning king in the household life, all that he seeks is swiftly attained.
If he leaves the home life to become a Buddha, all manner of offerings will be fully provided according to his every thought.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
How does one practice so as to have skin that is fine and soft, and not to receive dust or grime?
In the past, when the Buddha was still an ordinary person, if śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, or householders came to me and asked me: "
"Venerable Sir!
What is called wholesome conduct?
And what is called unwholesome?"
What should one associate with?
What should one distance oneself from?
Through what kind of conduct does one obtain peace and happiness?
"What kind of karmic actions lead to suffering and affliction?

In the past, for the sake of human beings, I distinguished that "this dharma should be done and this should not be done; this dharma should be practiced and this should not be practiced; this dharma leads to happiness and this dharma leads to lack of peace and joy."

By virtue of this karma, he accumulated immeasurable practices until reaching the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), where he enjoyed celestial blessings and happiness;
subsequently descending to the human realm, he attained the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*), his skin becoming fine and soft, such that it was not defiled by dust or water.
For example, although a lotus flower is in the water, the water cannot defile it;
the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are likewise so.

Because of these marks, if he were a householder, he would become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin), possessed of intelligence and wisdom such that no śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, or householders in any world could equal him.

If one leaves the household life to study the Way and attains Buddhahood, their wisdom will be vast and expansive; their swift and penetrating wisdom will be supreme and most excellent, such that among all gods, worldlings, Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, no one possessing wisdom can equal it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"For immeasurable eons, while practicing as an ordinary person,
if anyone came to question me, I diligently instructed them so they might quickly achieve success."
Constantly dwelling in the state of renunciation, they skillfully discern the meaning and intent [of the teachings].
By virtue of such karmic conduct, whether among the devas or among humans, they always attain great wisdom;
even when born as a human in this life, they possess it.
One attains skin that is fine and soft.
By virtue of these marks and signs, one achieves great wisdom.
If born into the Kṣatriya caste, one becomes a wheel-turning monarch remaining at home;
Having left the household life, one attains Buddhahood and acquires the knowledge of all modes;
among gods and humans alike, there is none who can equal them.
*Upāsikā-viśuddha-caryā-dharmaparyāya-sūtra*, Fascicle One.
*The Scripture on the Dharma-Gate of Pure Conduct for Upāsikās*, Scroll Lower.
Recorded by Sengyou as one of the "Extraordinary Scriptures from the Liang Territory" by Master Dao'an; appended to the Northern Liang Record.
The Remainder of the Second Chapter, "Cultivation and Study."
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
How does one practice so as to have a body of golden hue, radiating brilliance like a mountain of gold?

In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Tathāgata constantly delighted in cultivating goodness; he was without anger or resentment. Even if sentient beings reviled him with foul language or struck him with blows, he was able to endure it all, giving rise to no malice or hatred."
He is constantly filled with shame and remorse, giving rise to thoughts of great compassion:
"All of this is the retribution for my past karma.
He always reproaches himself.
Furthermore, he practiced giving, constantly bestowing upon others such garments as soft woolen rugs, kusha grass cloth, cotton cloth, and kshauma silk.
Thus, through successive transmigrations throughout immeasurable worlds, he accumulated vast merit and constantly experienced celestial bliss;
when descending to be born among humans, he attained the marks of a great man, his body being golden in color, the most supreme and excellent among all golden hues.

By virtue of these marks, if he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (cakravartin) ruling over the four continents; within those four continents, whatever soft items there may be—woolen rugs, bedding, kṣauma cloth, kārpāsa cotton, kauśeya silk, or kambala wool—the King shall obtain them all.
If he leaves the household life, he will attain Buddhahood; as for the fine and soft garments, bedding, kārpāsa, kṣauma, and kambala cloths of humans, the Tathāgata shall obtain all such things.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Without giving rise to a mind of anger, Constantly feeling shame and reproaching oneself,
One gives fine and exquisite garments, And superior, priceless cotton cloths.”
Constantly bestowing gifts upon sentient beings, their hearts rejoice after giving;
they leap for joy without stinginess,
like a person who, when a fire breaks out, feels great delight at rescuing their possessions.
Born in heaven, one experiences happiness; from there, one is born into the human realm and attains the marks of a great man.
One’s body is golden in color, like the king of golden mountains; as a householder, one becomes a wheel-turning monarch.
He shall well protect the four continents and obtain a most supple touch;
a single robe shall be worth ten million pieces of gold.
If he studies the Way and attains Buddhahood, transforming devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits, his robes shall likewise be so.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā! How does he practice to attain the mark of the horse’s sheath?

In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, when the Tathāgata was a common person, he always delighted in practicing the art of skillfully harmonizing groups. Whether it was with parents, sons, daughters, brothers, sisters, relatives, kinsmen, good friends, or acquaintances—even down to animals—if there were those who suffered separation and desired reunion, he would always act according to their wishes, skillfully bringing them together and causing them to rejoice."
By virtue of this karma, the merit he accumulated was so high and vast that he was constantly reborn in the heavens, receiving celestial blessings and joys;

when descending to be born among humans, he did so in such a manner for immeasurable and boundless lifetimes until reaching the stage of "one birth remaining" (ekajātipratibaddha), where he attained the mark of the horse's sheath (aśvakośa).

By virtue of these marks, it is prophesied that he will become a wheel-turning monarch with a thousand sons who rule over the four continents; these thousand sons will be brave and strong, capable of subduing enemies.
If he leaves the household life, he will attain Buddhahood; from the Dharma he will father more than ten million sons, who will be courageous and powerful, capable of repelling the enmity of Māra.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In immeasurable ages past, when I was originally an ordinary person,
I constantly acted as a unifier for the assembly, enabling them to dwell in peace and happiness."
Whether it be parents, sons, or daughters, brothers and sisters,
kinsmen and various relatives, or virtuous friends and spiritual teachers—
if there is the suffering of separation from them, may they be well united and at peace.
By virtue of these karmic deeds, one is constantly born among devas and humans;
experiencing celestial bliss, when reborn below in the human realm,
one attains the mark of the sheathed male organ.
Brave and peerless, he is able to subdue all enemies;
He constantly makes offerings to his parents, causing them to attain joy and happiness.
If he leaves the household life to become a Buddha, His sons and disciples shall number in the thousands.
Through the power of precepts, meditative concentration, and supernormal knowledges,
one is able to crush and subdue the host of Māra’s enemies. "Furthermore, Viśākhā,
how does one practice so that the body of Brahmā is perfected— standing as upright as a nyagrodha tree, with hands reaching down to touch the knees?"

When the Tathāgata was formerly a common person, he constantly cultivated great compassion and was skillfully able to observe the distinctions between good and evil, coarse and subtle, equal and unequal phenomena. He discerned: "This is wisdom, this is folly; this is diligence, this is indolence; this is anger, this is patience. Having made such distinctions, he instructed others according to their respective categories.
By virtue of this karma, he passed through immeasurable successions of births among devas and humans, up to the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood" (ekajātipratibaddha).
When descending to be born in the human realm, he attained two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*):
first, his Brahma-body was perfectly full, like a *nyagrodha* tree.
Second, his body is upright and straight, and his hands reach down to his knees.

By virtue of this mark, if he remains a householder, he becomes a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) who rules over the four continents; his wealth is immeasurable, consisting of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, pearls, and other jewels, while the five grains ripen in abundance and his treasuries overflow.
If he leaves the household life, he attains Buddhahood and becomes fully endowed with the seven riches.
"Faith, precepts, generosity, learning, wisdom, shame, and remorse—the Tathāgata also possesses such qualities as these, immeasurable and boundless.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"In past ages, I skillfully weighed and measured sentient beings."
Having made distinctions through discernment, one observes all things as equal.
Being able to constantly distinguish between sentient beings, one bestows gifts according to their respective types.
By virtue of such karmic actions, one is always reborn among gods and humans.
Reborn below among humans, his person stands upright and not crooked;
both hands reach down to touch his knees, just like the *nyagrodha* tree, which grows from the ground with perfect symmetry; the Buddha’s body is likewise so.
From immeasurable kalpas past, born from the ground of karmic deeds,
two signs have appeared as wealth, bringing peace and stability to the world.
Dwelling at home and enjoying the five desires, he has attained the status of a Wheel-Turning King.
"Having renounced the five desires and left the household life, he attained the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Furthermore, Viśākhā,
how does one cultivate the three marks of a Great Man?"
First, a lion-like chest;
second, light radiating from the back of the neck;
third, rounded shoulders and neck.

When the Tathāgata was a common person in the past, he constantly benefited sentient beings, delighting in dwelling in peace and happiness; with faith, he upheld the precepts, practiced much learning, and gave generously through wisdom. He caused his wealth, grain, fields, houses, slaves, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, carriages, wives, concubines, male and female attendants, retinues on the left and right, and kinsmen to increase and flourish.
By virtue of this karma, he was constantly reborn in the heavens;
when descending to be born among humans, he attained three marks of a great man:
first, a chest like that of a lion.
Second, light radiates from his neck;
third, his shoulders and neck are perfectly rounded.

Because of these marks, if he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents. His Dharma will constantly flourish, and his wealth, fields, houses, and the five grains will be abundant. He will be fully endowed with wife, children, kinsmen, servants, attendants, virtuous friends, and wise associates, with nothing lacking.
"If one leaves the household life, they shall attain Buddhahood; endowed with the seven riches, their fourfold assembly of followers shall never diminish.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Faith, upholding the precepts, Extensive learning, wisdom, and generosity— As for slaves, elephants, horses,"
Regarding cattle, sheep, fields, and houses, as well as one's wife, children, and kinsmen, and virtuous friends and spiritual mentors—
how may one constantly cultivate wholesome thoughts so that their physical strength, vitality,
and well-being may increase greatly?
By virtue of this karma, he was constantly reborn in the heavens and, when descending to be born among humans, attained the marks of a great man:
a chest like that of a half-lion, a neck from which light radiates like the sun, and shoulders and a neck that are perfectly rounded and straight—thus these three marks were perfected.
If one remains a householder, one's kinsmen, wife, children, servants, elephants, and horses will all flourish;
if one leaves the home life, one shall attain Buddhahood, one’s retinue will increase, and one will obtain the quality of non-decrease.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
How does one practice so as to have the svastika mark upon the chest?
In the past, when the Tathāgata was still an ordinary person, he did not afflict sentient beings, did not employ the use of canes or whips, nor did he imprison or bind them."
By virtue of these karmic actions, his accumulated conduct became lofty and vast, and he was constantly reborn in the heavens;
when descending to be born among humans, he attained the marks of a great man, with a svastika upon his chest.
If he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), free from all diseases; the four seasons will be harmonious, being neither too cold nor too hot.

If he leaves the home life, he will attain Buddhahood; likewise, he will be free from all ailments, always remaining in a state of equilibrium, neither cold nor hot, his body light and agile, capable of entering samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Do not cage or bind sentient beings, Nor inflict the punishment of whips or canes;
Do not use various blades or staves To cause harm to sentient beings."
By virtue of these deeds, one is constantly reborn among devas and humans,
experiencing celestial bliss until reaching the stage of "one birth remaining" (ekajātipratibaddha).
When descending to be born in the human realm, one attains the marks of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa).
The character "chest" contains ten thousand numerical units;
it brings no illnesses whatsoever, and whether one is a householder or a renunciant,
one shall always experience happiness.
If one is born into the Kṣatriya caste, one shall rule over the four continents;
if one leaves the household life to study the Way, one shall attain the status of the Unsurpassed Honored One and experience exclusively sublime bliss.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
How does one practice so that the area below the eyes becomes deep blue like a blue lotus, with eyelashes curled upward and emitting a deep blue radiance?"

In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, when the Buddha was a common person, he constantly cultivated wholesome deeds. He never cast his gaze upon sentient beings with an evil mind, nor did he look down upon them with averted eyes; he never glanced at them with a lustful mind. Rather, he always looked directly at sentient beings with a joyful heart, free from hatred, attachment, and delusion.
By virtue of this karma, he was constantly reborn in the heavens, where he experienced celestial bliss;
when subsequently born among humans, he obtained two marks of a great man:
first, the area beneath his eyes was deep blue, and both the upper and lower eyelids could blink simultaneously.
Second, his eyelashes are fine and soft, curled upward, long, and possess a deep blue radiance.

Because of this mark, if he remains a householder, he becomes a Wheel-Turning King who rules over the four continents; all the people—including śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, householders, wives, children, retinues, ministers, and attendants—will gaze upon him without weariness.

If he leaves the home life, he attains Buddhahood; the fourfold assembly (bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās), devas, humans, asuras, mahoragas, gandharvas, and all other sentient beings will look upon the Tathāgata with virtuous joy and never tire of gazing at him.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When the Buddha was in past ages, While originally a common man,
He constantly cultivated all wholesome deeds, Never with a mind of anger."
Opening the eyes, one casts down the gaze and does not look upon sentient beings with a mind stained by desire.
With eyes pure and free from defilement, one looks straight ahead with a joyful heart.
Constantly born among devas and humans, reaching the stage of being "one birth away from Buddhahood," he will descend to be born in the human realm; his eyelashes will be deep blue,
his eyes like the blue lotus, with both upper and lower lashes blinking with brilliant clarity.
By these marks of a Great Man, he is prophesied to possess intelligence and wisdom;
all sentient beings will delight in beholding him, never wearying of the sight.
As a Wheel-Turning King remaining at home, he shall achieve great wisdom.
Fully endowed with the seven treasures, he was able to subdue the four continents;
having left the household life, he attained Buddhahood and acquired all-encompassing wisdom.
Furthermore, Viśākhā!
How does one practice so as to have a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon the crown of the head and hair of deep blue-black color?

When the Tathāgata was a common person in past lives, he was always foremost among those of merit; through his physical, verbal, and mental actions, he practiced giving and upheld the precepts, observed the six fast days each month, and made offerings to his parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, friends, kinsmen, elders, and venerable seniors, as well as performing other virtuous deeds beyond measure.
By virtue of these practices, they accumulate immeasurable merit and constantly enjoy celestial pleasures until reaching the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood;
when descending to be born among humans, they obtain two marks of a great man:
first, a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) upon the crown of the head.
Second, his hair is deep blue-black.
Because of this mark, if he remains at home, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, serving as a refuge for all the people;

if he leaves the home life, he will attain Buddhahood and become a place of reliance for the fourfold assembly (bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās), as well as for devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In past lives, I was the foremost leader among those who cultivated goodness;
I constantly practiced and maintained the pure conduct (brahmacarya), serving as a refuge for all people."
At the end of life, he was reborn in the heavens, where he experienced all celestial joys;
later descending to be born among humans, he attained two marks of a Great Man:
a fleshy protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) upon his crown, and hair that is curled and deep blue-black.
As a wheel-turning monarch dwelling at home, he rules over the four continents;
by means of the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths of action, he protects and shelters the people.
If he leaves the home life to study the Way, he attains the state of the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Constantly employing precept, concentration, and wisdom, you instruct all sentient beings;
you always serve as a place of refuge for devas and humans,
nāgas, yakṣas, and the like, as well as for gandharvas and asuras.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
How does one practice so that a single hair grows from each and every pore, and the white tuft between the eyebrows is like *tūla* cotton?

In the past, when the Buddha was an ordinary person, he practiced non-false speech, abandoned false speech, constantly cultivated truthful speech, maintained truthful speech, spoke with a correct mind and truthfully, refrained from frivolous chatter, and his words were gentle and compliant with sentient beings."
By virtue of this karma, he was constantly reborn in the heavens, experiencing celestial bliss;
when later born in the human realm, he obtained two marks of a great man:
first, from each and every pore grows a single hair, these hairs being fine and soft, all curling to the right, and repelling both dust and water.
Second, the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows is brilliant and lustrous, like *tūla* cotton.

Because of this mark, if he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) ruling over the four continents; all his subjects will flourish and increase, and their happiness will be boundless.

If he leaves the household life, he will attain Buddhahood; he will cause the fourfold assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen to increase, becoming immeasurable and limitless, filling the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In past lives, I constantly cultivated truthful speech;
My mouth never once uttered empty, deceptive, or unreal words."
Acting in accordance with the world, his speech is free from fault.
By virtue of such conduct, he is always born among gods and humans;
when descending to be born in the human realm, he attains two marks of a Great Man.
The white tuft of hair between his brows is as soft as *tūla* cotton;
from each pore there arises no second, and each one curls to the right.
By virtue of these two marks, he may become a Wheel-Turning King while remaining at home.
Universally ruling over the four continents, he causes the people to flourish;
if he renounces the household life to study the Way, he becomes a Great Dharma King,
instructing all devas and humans so that the True Dharma increases.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
How does one practice so as to have forty teeth that are white, even, and closely set?

In the past, throughout immeasurable kalpas, the Tathāgata constantly cultivated non-divisive speech; he abandoned divisive speech, remained far removed from it, and having heard something from this person, did not repeat it to that person, nor having heard it from that person, did he repeat it to this person. Only after hearing from both parties, and finding it to be beneficial and conducive to joy, would he speak of it."
By virtue of this karma, he constantly experiences celestial bliss;
when reborn in the human realm, he attains two marks of a great man:
first, his mouth has forty teeth.
Second, his teeth are white, even, and closely set.

Because of this mark, if he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) ruling over the four continents; there will be no thieves or robbers, his retinue will be pure, and he will be firm and indestructible.

If he leaves the home life to become a Buddha, he will obtain the fourfold assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, who will firmly uphold the Tathāgata’s treasury of the Dharma and cannot be defeated by the four Māras.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“In past lives, the Tathāgata practiced refraining from divisive speech;
he did not incite strife among sentient beings, but was skillful at harmonizing the multitude.”
Through these karmic actions, one is born in the heavens and experiences celestial bliss;
later descending to be born among humans, one attains two marks of a great man:
the mouth possesses forty teeth, which are white, pure, even, and closely set.
If one is born into the kṣatriya caste, dwelling at home as a king over the four continents,
possessing a royal army of four divisions that is firm and difficult to destroy,
then even kṣatriyas and brahmins can never move him from his place.
"If one leaves the household life to become a Buddha, the fourfold assembly will likewise be so;
they shall be honored and respected by all devas and humans.
Furthermore, Viśākhā:
How does one cultivate the mark of the broad and long tongue and produce a Brahma-like voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird?
In the past, when the Buddha was an ordinary person, he did not engage in harsh speech; he abandoned harsh speech and remained far removed from it.
He constantly cultivated virtuous and gentle speech that could penetrate the hearts of others.
He causes them to delight in hearing words of great compassion, words that do not abandon others, and words of vast grace—words beloved by all people.
By virtue of this karma, he diligently accumulates merit so lofty and expansive that he constantly experiences celestial bliss;
when later born among humans, he attains two marks of a Great Man:
First, his broad and long tongue can extend out to cover his entire face;
second, his Brahma-voice is soft and supple like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, causing people to delight in hearing it.

By virtue of these marks, if he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents; whatever he says will be joyfully heard by all the people, who will receive and uphold it with delight.

If he does not delight in the household life and leaves home to study the Path, he will attain Buddhahood; and whatever he speaks, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others will all receive it upon their heads and joyfully practice it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"In past lives, the Buddha constantly practiced virtuous speech;
He was neither angry nor resentful, Nor did he engage in quarreling, strife, or harsh words."
Always practicing speech of loving-kindness and compassion, resolute, correct, and gentle—
speaking with such single-minded harmony, one then utters words.
By virtue of these karmic actions, one attains the mark of a broad and long tongue.
His Brahma-voice is pure and gentle, like the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
With these two marks of a great man, he would be a wheel-turning monarch if remaining at home;
whatever he might say, all the people would receive and practice.
Having left the household life, he attained Buddhahood and was able to turn the unsurpassed wheel;
as for the sublime Dharma he preached, gods, humans, asuras, nāgas,
