spirits, yakṣas, and others— all who heard it followed and practiced it.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā! How does one practice the 'lion's neck'?
When the Buddha was an ordinary person in past lives, he constantly cultivated the avoidance of frivolous speech, renounced frivolous speech, and remained far removed from frivolous speech."
He speaks at the appropriate time, speaking with meaning, speaking in accordance with the Dharma, speaking with dignified decorum, speaking words of permanence, and speaking with purpose.
By virtue of these deeds, he accumulates immeasurable merit and constantly experiences celestial bliss;
when descending to be born among humans, he attains the mark of a Great Man: a jaw like that of a lion.
By virtue of these marks, if he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, such that no people whatsoever shall be able to conquer him;

if he leaves the household life, he will attain Buddhahood, such that among devas, humans, asuras, brahmas, māras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or internal and external enemies, none shall be able to overcome the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"In past lives, I constantly cultivated the avoidance of frivolous speech;
I neither praised myself nor engaged in various kinds of idle chatter."
Having severed speech that is meaningless, one should always cultivate speech that is timely;
by speaking words that bring joy and delight, one benefits all sentient beings.
Through these karmic actions, one constantly experiences the pleasures of devas and humans.
Descending to be born among humans, he achieves the lion’s jaw.
As a wheel-turning monarch in the household, his majesty subdues the four continents;
by virtue of this mark of a great man, there is none who can attack him.
Having left the household life, one attains Buddhahood;
as a śramaṇa, one is invincible before Brahmā, Māra, devas, humans, asuras, Rāhus, kiṃnaras, and all enemies, both internal and external. No one is able to conquer him.
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
How does one cultivate the four canine teeth that are even, closely set, white, pure, and radiant?

In the past, when the Buddha was a common person, he abandoned wrong livelihood and sustained himself through right livelihood. He did not practice deception with measures or scales, nor did he seize the property of others by force or intimidation. He did not deceive people with counterfeit goods, nor did he employ deception regarding form, deception regarding affection, deception regarding touch, or deception regarding diligence. All such methods of deception were entirely eradicated."
By virtue of this karma, which was accumulated to great height and breadth, at the end of his life he was reborn in the heavens, where he experienced pleasure in ten places among the devas.
What are these ten?
First, celestial longevity;
Second, celestial exquisite form;
third, celestial pleasure;
fourth, celestial renown.
Fifth, the celestial king;
sixth, the celestial form;
seventh, the celestial voice;
Eighth, celestial fragrance;
ninth, celestial flavor;
tenth, celestial touch.
These are called the ten.
Having experienced celestial bliss, he is born again among humans and attains the marks of a great man:
first, his teeth are neither too large nor too small.
Second, his teeth are white and pure.

Because of this mark, if he remains a householder, he will become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents; his fourfold army, the assemblies of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, the villages, towns, and cities, the ministers and elders, the queens, concubines, and all his thousand sons will all be strictly pure.

If he leaves the household life, he will attain Buddhahood; likewise, his fourfold assembly (bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās), as well as devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others, will all be pure.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"In past lives, I abandoned all forms of wrong livelihood;
By means of the benefit of the pure Dharma, I cultivated right livelihood for my own sustenance."
Able to remove the suffering of sentient beings, Causing them to attain peace and happiness.
By virtue of these deeds, One experiences the ten kinds of celestial bliss,
And is always honored and praised by all devas and humans.
Having enjoyed such pleasures, he was reborn in the human world;
moved by the accumulation of his karma, he attained two marks of a Great Man:
his teeth were neither coarse nor fine, and the color of his tusks was radiant, white, and pure.
If he attains birth in the Kṣatriya caste, he will be a Wheel-Turning King at home,
surrounded by the fourfold army, pure and free from defilement;
if he leaves the household life to become a Buddha, he will always be attended by the fourfold assembly.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās,
devas, humans, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, and others—
pure and free from defilement— all respectfully surround him.
“Viśākhā! These are called the twenty practices by which one attains the thirty-two marks of a great man.
By means of these marks, the subtle and wondrous body of the Tathāgata is adorned.”
"Furthermore, Viśākhā!
The Buddha’s body also possesses eighty secondary marks (anuvyañjana).
What are these eighty secondary marks called? [They are as follows:]"
First, the fingernails are crimson;
second, the fingernails are convex;
third, the fingernails are smooth and clean.
Fourth, the nails are complete;
fifth, the fingers are rounded;
sixth, the fingers are slender and straight.
Seventh, the spaces between the fingers are close-set;
eighth, the fingers are clean and pure;
ninth, the hands and feet are supple and lustrous.
Tenth, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet are red;
eleventh, the hands and feet are symmetrical;
twelfth, the interiors of the hands and feet are full.
Thirteenth, the lines on the palms appear deep;
fourteenth, the lines on the palms are straight and upright;
fifteenth, the lines on the palms are slender and long.
Sixteenth, his hands and feet are moist and lustrous;
seventeenth, the lines on his palms are unconfused;
eighteenth, his ankle bones do not protrude.
19. His kneecaps are perfectly rounded;
20. His knees are successively well-filled;
21. His gait is even and upright.
Twenty-two: the gait of the lion king;
twenty-three: the gait of the goose king;
twenty-four: the characteristics of the gait of the dragon king.
Twenty-five: the gait of a bull king;
twenty-six: walking without looking back;
twenty-seven: walking with unconfused steps.
Twenty-eighth, his body is upright;
twenty-ninth, the Buddha’s body surpasses that of ordinary men;
thirtieth, all [faculties] are fully perfected.
31. The Buddha’s body is entirely excellent;
32. His body is level and upright;
33. His body is fully developed.
34. The body is straight; 35. the body is smooth and lustrous;
36. the parts of the body are proportionate in size.
37. The body is pure and clean;
38. The body is supple; 39. The body is tranquil.
Forty: the body is slender; forty-one: the body is compact;
forty-two: the body is upright and majestic.
43. His sense organs are well-proportioned;
44. his bodily complexion is not dark; 45.
his body is free from moles or blemishes.
46. The body hairs are clean and pure;
47. the abdomen is rounded; 48.
the abdomen is free of horizontal folds.
Forty-ninth, the body is luminous and pure, clearly perceiving all forms and images;
fiftieth, the navel is deep;
fifty-first, the opening of the navel is perfectly round.
Fifty-two: the navel is spiraled to the right;
fifty-three: the navel cavity is not sunken;
fifty-four: the opening of the navel is not elongated.
Fifty-five: the navel opening is not short;
fifty-six: the navel hair extends downward in connection;
fifty-seven: he possesses the mark of dragon-teeth.
Fifty-eight: His canine teeth do not protrude beyond his lips;
fifty-nine: His four canine teeth are rounded;
sixty: His four canine teeth are sharp.
Sixty-first, his four canine teeth are slender and long;
sixty-second, his four canine teeth are even and closely set;
sixty-third, his tongue is broad and supple.
Sixty-fourth, the color of the tongue is a beautiful red;
sixty-fifth, the voice is deep and wondrous like that of Brahmā;
sixty-sixth, the voice is like that of a king elephant.
Sixty-seven: A voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird;
sixty-eight: The flesh at the base of the teeth is full;
sixty-nine: The nose does not sag downward.
Seventy: His nose is high and long;
seventy-one: His nostrils are pure and clean;
seventy-two: His nose is long, straight, and broad.
Seventy-three: His eyes are beautiful, expansive, and smooth and pure both inside and out;
seventy-four: His pupils are black and lustrous;
seventy-five: His eyelashes are well-ordered.
Seventy-sixth: His eyebrows are like half-moons, with rounded contours and long, extended arches;
seventy-seventh: His eyebrows are jet-black and lustrous, their lengths following one another in proper order;
seventy-eighth: His eyebrows are of a pure color, smooth, clean, and radiant.
Seventy-ninth: His ears are long and hang down, being pure both inside and out;
eightieth: His hair is fine and soft, curling to the right without disorder, growing in orderly, slender strands, all of which are excellent.
"Viśākhā! These are called the eighty secondary marks of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"One who for a long night upholds all the prohibitive precepts and performs immeasurable ascetic practices is called a Great Brahmin.
Adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, his body is like a jeweled necklace; he is the most honored among gods and humans."
The radiance was brilliant and intense, shining boundlessly; blue, yellow, red, and white intermingled with one another.
It swirled and rose up, filling all of empty space, emitting great light that illuminated immeasurable realms.
The light from within shines brilliantly throughout the three thousandfold world-system; the Tathāgata’s constant radiance illuminates a space of one fathom.
When he emits great beams of light, the sun and moon are eclipsed, just as when the sun rises, the various stars do not appear.
If he emits light from his middle [body], illuminating the world, the radiance of the sun is like that of the moon, and the radiance of the moon is like that of a star.
For the sake of all sentient beings, it is what they joyfully behold; they gaze upon it with delight.
"I am never satiated. **Chapter Three:

Signs of Auspicious Response** *The Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of the Pure Conduct of Upāsikās* At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the Mother of Viśākhā was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. She addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"When the Bodhisattva was dwelling in the womb and at the time of his birth, how many extraordinary and subtle signs appeared in the world?
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"At the time of the Bodhisattva’s birth, there were sixteen kinds of extraordinary and auspicious signs."
What are the sixteen kinds of marks?

They are as follows: that the Bodhisattva, having relinquished his body in Tuṣita Heaven, dwells in his mother’s womb with clear and distinct mindfulness; this is the first unprecedented and marvelous dharma.

"When the Bodhisattva, having relinquished his celestial body, dwells within the womb, a natural radiance illuminates the world. Even those regions between worlds that are dark and obscure—places where the light of the sun, moon, and stars cannot reach—become entirely bright. The sentient beings therein are each able to see one another and all say:
'How is it that sentient beings have suddenly appeared here? Among all the lights of the entire world, including those of the Brahmās, Māras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, none can equal this! "
Furthermore, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and all the Mount Sumerus trembled incessantly; this was the second unprecedented and marvelous phenomenon.

"While the Bodhisattva dwells in the womb, four celestial sons maintain majestic deportment, attending upon and guarding the Bodhisattva and his mother from all four directions, ensuring that neither humans nor non-humans can cause them harm; this is the third unprecedented and marvelous phenomenon."

"When a Bodhisattva dwells in the womb, he can cause his mother to naturally observe the precepts—refraining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking alcohol. This is the first of four unprecedented and marvelous dharmas."

"While the Bodhisattva dwells in the womb, his mother remains pure and free from desire; even when outsiders see her, they do not give rise to defiled thoughts—this is the fifth unprecedented and marvelous phenomenon."

"While the Bodhisattva dwells in the womb, he always causes his mother to receive great offerings; forms, fragrances, tastes, and textures arrive spontaneously. This is the sixth unprecedented and marvelous phenomenon."
"While the Bodhisattva dwells in the womb, the mother is constantly at peace and free from all ailments, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, or the suffering of exhaustion; the Bodhisattva is likewise."

While the Bodhisattva is within the womb, his mother sees him constantly, just as one might hold in the palm of one's hand a genuine maṇi-vaiḍūrya gem—octagonal, pure, transparent both inside and out, and complete in every respect—which has been strung with threads of five colors. A person with clear vision, holding it in their hand, clearly and distinctly perceives the eight facets of the gem as well as the five-colored threads: blue, yellow, red, and white.

The Bodhisattva’s dwelling in the womb is likewise so; the mother sees his body, head, eyes, hands, feet, and all his limbs entirely without obstruction—this is the seventh unprecedented and marvelous phenomenon.

“Viśākhā! Seven days after the Bodhisattva was born, his mother’s life came to an end and she was reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where she enjoys celestial bliss; this is the eighth unprecedented and marvelous phenomenon.”
“Ordinary people undergo conception and give birth after nine months or up to ten months;
the Bodhisattva is not like this, for he is born only after the full ten months have elapsed. This is the ninth unprecedented and marvelous quality.”
"When women of the world are about to give birth, their bodies suffer pain; they are restless whether sitting or lying down, and only then is the child born.

When the Bodhisattva was born, his mother was peaceful and at ease, free from all illness or distress; she played with joy as he was born standing upright with his hands raised. This is the tenth unprecedented and marvelous phenomenon."
"When the Bodhisattva emerges from the womb, celestial beings receive him, after which he is held up by the people of the world; this is the eleventh extraordinary phenomenon.
Once the people have received him, four heavenly kings receive and respectfully hold him, placing him before his mother with great joy, and they all cry out in unison:
'Excellent, O Lady!'"
"He shall give birth to a son of great majesty, valor, and strength.
These are the twelve extraordinary phenomena.

"When the Bodhisattva was first born, there was no water, blood, placenta, or any other impure substances; his body was pure like a *maṇi* jewel, and when wrapped in cloth from the kingdom of Kāśi, it remained unstained by them."
Why is this? Because both are pure.

It is likewise with the Bodhisattva’s first birth: he is pure and unstained like a maṇi jewel, and his mother is fresh and pure like that fine cotton cloth; this is the thirteenth extraordinary phenomenon.
"When the Bodhisattva was born, two streams of water spontaneously appeared in the sky:
one cold and one warm, which bathed the Bodhisattva’s body; this is the fourteenth extraordinary phenomenon."

"When the Bodhisattva was born, he walked seven steps toward the north. At that time, a white parasol spontaneously appeared in the air to cover the Bodhisattva’s body. Having taken these seven steps, he surveyed the ten directions and uttered a lion’s roar, declaring:
'In all the world, I alone am supreme; among gods and humans, I am the most honored; I am the greatest. From this birth, it is the end; there shall be no further rebirth!'"
These are the fifteen extraordinary qualities.
"When the Bodhisattva was born, all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm, including even the crawling insects, were filled with great joy; this is the sixteenth extraordinary quality."
“Viśākhā! These are called the sixteen kinds of extraordinary phenomena concerning the Tathāgata’s dwelling in the womb and his initial birth.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Having passed away from Tuṣita Heaven, he descended to be born among humans;
dwelling in the womb and at his initial birth, he was pure and unstained.
Sixteen kinds of wonders, subtle and marvelous, such as had never occurred before,"
While in the womb and at the time of birth, he was not shared with other sentient beings;
at birth, he was without confusion, his fame being foremost.
The manifested signs were of no single kind—such are the auspicious omens of a Buddha’s birth.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the Mother Viśākhā was filled with great joy and asked further:
"World-Honored One!
When a Bodhisattva is born, how many auspicious signs appear simultaneously?"
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
"When the Bodhisattva was born, thirty-two auspicious signs appeared simultaneously.
What are these thirty-two auspicious signs?"
First, the earth of the trichiliocosm shook violently, and a natural, great radiance illuminated the world;
second, all musical instruments spontaneously produced music;
third, drums sounded without being struck.
Fourth, all illnesses will naturally be cured;
fifth, all bonds will naturally be released;
sixth, all enemies will give rise to a heart of compassion.
Seventh, those born blind shall gain eyes and be able to see all forms;
eighth, those born deaf shall gain ears and be able to hear sounds;
ninth, those born lame shall be able to walk, roaming and playing at will.
Tenth, those born insane regained their mindfulness, and their recollections became clear;
eleventh, the mute were able to speak;
twelfth, those adrift on ships returned to their original places.
Thirteenth, all the seven treasures on the earth and in the void spontaneously radiate light;
fourteenth, the myriad rivers and ten thousand streams cease their flow and remain still;
fifteenth, all flying birds and winged creatures dwell there in joy.
Sixteenth, the winds ceased their agitation, and all became tranquil;
seventeenth, all sentient beings who were devouring one another gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness;
eighteenth, all the devas returned to their palaces, filled with joy, laughter, and happiness.
Nineteenth, the fierce fires of the Avīci Hell extinguish themselves;
twentieth, the hungry obtain full satisfaction;
twenty-first, none among all the *preta*s suffer from thirst or exhaustion.
Twenty-second, great clouds arise everywhere over the four continents, pouring down rain equally;
twenty-third, the moon shines with brilliant radiance;
twenty-fourth, the various stars appear during the day.
Twenty-fifth, the sun became exceptionally bright and clear;
twenty-sixth, all flowering trees immediately blossomed;
twenty-seventh, all fruit-bearing trees naturally bore fruit.
Twenty-eighth, a great celestial fragrance pervades the trichiliocosm, free from any foul odors;
twenty-ninth, at the time of his birth, the Bodhisattva immediately takes seven steps;
thirtieth, a white parasol spontaneously appears in the empty sky to provide shade and protection.
Thirty-first, having taken seven steps, he gazes upon the ten directions;
thirty-second, he utters the lion’s roar. Viśākhā!
"This is called the manifestation of thirty-two dharmas simultaneously at the time of a bodhisattva’s first birth.
The mother Viśākhā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“By what causes and conditions does the trichiliocosm shake when a Bodhisattva is born?
The Buddha told Viśākhā:
“When the earth shakes violently at the time of a Bodhisattva’s birth, it is because the Bodhisattva manifests that this is his final birth and that he will have no further afflictions.”
Vaiśākha! All sentient beings who are destined to attain the Way have their afflictions about to be extinguished;
for this reason, the earth trembles.
When a Bodhisattva is born, natural radiance illuminates the world because the Bodhisattva has attained the three types of supernormal knowledge.
Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, the musical instruments of the world resounded spontaneously because the Bodhisattva had attained eight samādhis. Viśākhā!
When the Bodhisattva was born, the drums sounded spontaneously without being struck; this was because the Bodhisattva desired to beat the great Dharma drum. Viśākhā!
When the Bodhisattva was born, all fetters were naturally liberated; this was because the Bodhisattva desired to deliver and liberate all sentient beings from old age, sickness, and death.
Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, all enemies gave rise to thoughts of loving-kindness because the Bodhisattva had attained the four immeasurable minds. Viśākhā!
When the Bodhisattva was born, those suffering from illness were healed; this was because the Bodhisattva desired to extinguish all diseases of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Viśākhā!
When the Bodhisattva was born, the blind regained their sight; this was because the Bodhisattva had attained the eye of noble wisdom (*āryajñānacakṣus*).
Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, those who were deaf regained their hearing because the Bodhisattva had attained the noble divine ear (divya-śrotra). Viśākhā!
When the Bodhisattva was born, those who were lame were able to walk; this was because the Bodhisattva had attained the power of the four bases of psychic mastery (*ṛddhipāda*). Viśākha!
When the Bodhisattva was born, those who were insane regained their mindfulness; this was because the Bodhisattva had attained mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, those who were mute were able to speak; this was because the Bodhisattva had attained thorough penetration of the dharmas known by the Tathāgata. Viśākhā!

When the Bodhisattva was born, those whose ships had drifted away returned; this was because the Bodhisattva had attained the Eightfold Noble Path and intended to reveal it to sentient beings. Viśākhā!

When the Bodhisattva was born, the earth and the sky were filled with the radiance of the seven treasures; this was because the Bodhisattva had attained the four types of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, the myriad rivers and streams stood still and ceased to flow because the Bodhisattva had already brought the four floods of affliction to a standstill.
Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, all the birds that dwell in joy were so because the Bodhisattva desired to destroy all false views. Viśākhā!
When the Bodhisattva was born, the winds did not stir because the Bodhisattva had attained the *nirvāṇa-samādhi* of eternal bliss. Viśākha!

When sentient beings who were devouring one another conceived thoughts of loving-kindness at the time of the Bodhisattva’s birth, it was because the Bodhisattva had attained the fourfold assembly, so that the high and low, the noble and the humble, might achieve harmony.

"Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, those devas who returned to their palaces and dwelt there with joyful laughter will, when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, become sons and daughters of good family who leave the home life to study the Way. They shall attain arhatship, accomplish what is to be done, sever the source of birth and death within the triple world, cast off the heavy burden, and dwell in the unconditioned and desireless state.

Always delighting in quietude, they will be radiant and smiling, saying to one another: 'We have now attained liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death; we shall no longer receive a womb-born existence or dwell within the cycle of birth and death. We are pure and undefiled, like a drop of water upon a lotus leaf, with nothing to which we are attached.'"

"Viśākhā! As for the fact that the fierce fires of the Avīci Hell were extinguished at the time of the Bodhisattva’s birth, it was because the Bodhisattva desired to extinguish the blazing fires of the three poisons and afflictions of sentient beings."
"Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, those who were hungry became fully satiated because the Bodhisattva had attained the samādhi of mindfulness of the body. Viśākhā!
When the Bodhisattva was born, the hungry ghosts who were parched with thirst were no longer thirsty, for the Bodhisattva had attained the water of liberation. Viśākha!
When great clouds poured down rain at the time of the Bodhisattva’s birth, it was because the Bodhisattva desired to rain down the great rain of the Dharma to universally moisten all sentient beings.
Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, the moon shone with brilliance; when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, it is for the sake of all sentient beings joyfully gazing upon him.
"Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, the stars appeared during the day; this was because when the Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood, he would cause his śrāvaka disciples to appear in the world."
Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, the sunlight was intensely brilliant because the Bodhisattva had attained the six supernormal powers as a Great Śrāvaka. Viśākhā!
When the Bodhisattva was born, the flowering trees blossomed; this was because the Bodhisattva intended for his śrāvaka disciples to obtain the flowers of liberation. Viśākha!
When the Bodhisattva was born, the fruit-bearing trees bore fruit; this was because the Bodhisattva intended for his śrāvaka disciples to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.

Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, the celestial fragrance that issued from the great trichiliocosm arose because the Bodhisattva had attained the Tathāgata’s fragrance of morality, which pervades the entire world.
Viśākhā! When the Bodhisattva was born, he took seven steps upon the earth because the Bodhisattva had attained the seven factors of enlightenment. Viśākhā!
When the Bodhisattva walks, he is shaded by a white parasol because the Bodhisattva has attained the shade of nirvāṇa.
Viśākha! When the Bodhisattva has walked and points toward the east, it is because he acts as a guide for all sentient beings.
"Viśākhā! The pointing toward the south is for the sake of acting as a noble field of merit for all sentient beings. Viśākhā!"
Pointing toward the west signifies that my births have been exhausted, for this is my final body. Viśākhā!
Pointing toward the north signifies that I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* for the sake of all sentient beings.
Viśākhā! As for the pointing toward the nadir, it is because he wishes to shatter the hosts of Māra’s army and cause them to retreat and disperse. Viśākhā!
He points toward the zenith because he is the one upon whom all devas and humans rely for refuge. Viśākhā!
One who utters the lion’s roar is the most honored and supreme among devas and humans, for no sentient being can equal him.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The foremost guide of the world, The unsurpassed, great, holy Honored One,
Manifested auspicious signs at birth, A field of merit for all sentient beings."
Transmigrating through the three realms, this is my final birth;
regarding wisdom in the world, the Tathāgata is foremost.
Having shattered the hosts of Māra’s army, he is the one of great renown who is worthy of offerings.
Unprecedented in the world, the refuge of devas and humans—
when the World-Honored One was first born, thirty-two auspicious omens,
with subtle and wondrous, extraordinary marks, all manifested simultaneously.
When the Bodhisattva was born from the womb, the earth shook in six ways;
a natural great radiance shone forth, illuminating the ten directions.
It caused the hair of all sentient beings to stand on end, and each spoke to the others, saying:
May you swiftly attain Buddhahood and rain down the great Dharma rain;
may you wash away the defilements of affliction and grant me liberation.
For this reason, I now take refuge in the Unsurpassed Honored One.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Viśākhā:

“The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are inconceivable; the Dharma taught by the Buddhas is inconceivable; the faith of good sons and good daughters in what the Buddhas have taught is also inconceivable; and the karmic fruits they obtain are likewise inconceivable.”
Just as a great rain moistens and nourishes all humans and non-humans alike, providing them with abundance, and causes all grasses and trees to grow, so too is the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata;
it universally moistens all immeasurable sentient beings.
Those who were ready for deliverance, having heard this Dharma, all attained the fruits of the Path;
as for those who were to receive retribution among humans or devas, they all obtained it according to their respective aspirations.
"Therefore, you should now single-mindedly receive and uphold this Dharma, so that in future ages all members of the fourfold assembly may attain its practice.

When this Dharma was spoken, sixty thousand devas and humans attained the pure Dharma-eye; the remaining devas, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others, all vowed to put it into practice.

Viśākhā attained the pure Dharma-eye; her retinue of fifteen hundred people likewise gained firm faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, never to regress. All were filled with great joy, paid their respects, and departed.
The Sūtra on the Dharma Gate of the Pure Conduct of Upāsikās, Scroll II.
